lesson.title: Nested Loops: A Loop Inside a Loop
lesson.summary: A nested loop is a loop placed inside the body of another loop, so the inner loop runs to completion on every single pass of the outer loop, which is the standard way to handle anything with two dimensions.
lesson.body:
A nested loop is exactly what it sounds like: one loop written inside the body of another. Because a loop body can contain any statements at all, and another loop is itself just a statement, there is nothing syntactically special about putting one inside the other. What matters is understanding the behavior it produces: for every single pass of the outer loop, the entire inner loop runs from start to finish before the outer loop is ever allowed to advance to its own next pass.

This means the total number of times the innermost code runs is the outer loop's repeat count multiplied by the inner loop's repeat count, not simply added together. Two outer passes with three inner passes each means the innermost line runs six times in total, not five, which is easy to underestimate before you have traced through an example carefully.

Here is a concrete example:
for row in range(1, 3):
    for col in range(1, 4):
        print(row, col)
Trace it layer by layer. When row is 1, the inner loop runs completely on its own from beginning to end: col becomes 1, printing "1 1"; col becomes 2, printing "1 2"; col becomes 3, printing "1 3"; then range(1, 4) is exhausted and the inner loop ends for this pass. Only then does the outer loop advance: row becomes 2, and the inner loop starts over completely fresh, with col again running through 1, 2, and 3, printing "2 1", "2 2", and "2 3" in turn. In total, six lines are printed, matching 2 outer passes times 3 inner passes exactly.

Nested loops are the standard approach whenever a problem naturally has two dimensions to it: printing a multiplication table, processing every cell in a grid or a matrix, or comparing every possible pair of items drawn from two separate lists. Each loop can also mix loop types freely, a for loop can contain a while loop and vice versa, and each one keeps its own independent loop variable and its own independent stopping condition, entirely separate from whatever the other loop is doing. Nesting is also not limited to two levels; a loop inside a loop inside another loop is perfectly legal, though the total number of passes multiplies at every additional level, so three loops each running ten times already means one thousand passes through the innermost body.

It is important to remember how break and continue behave inside nested loops. Each one only affects the loop it is directly written inside, never further out than that. A break inside the inner loop ends only that inner loop for the current outer pass, letting the outer loop continue on as normal afterward; it does not reach out and stop the outer loop too. Keeping this scoping firmly in mind is essential once your loops start nesting, since assuming a break or continue reaches further than its own immediate loop is a common source of subtle, confusing bugs.
